concept.name: Terminal shakeout
concept.definition: A large, decisive version of a spring occurring at the end of an accumulation trading range, in which price breaks sharply below support and rapidly recovers, forcing the final transfer of shares from weak holders to large operators. The tutorial describes it as 'a spring on steroids'.
concept.intuition: The last violent flush that scares out everyone still holding, right before the real move up begins.
concept.mechanics: Like a spring, a terminal shakeout takes price below the range low late in the range, but with a deeper or more dramatic break and a fast, forceful recovery; a subsequent low-volume test of the shakeout low confirms that supply has been exhausted and the stock is ready to be marked up.
concept.failure_modes: A deep break that fails to recover quickly is a genuine breakdown, not a shakeout; the label is only validated by the speed of recovery and a successful low-volume test afterward.
concept.misconceptions: Terminal shakeouts are not required for accumulation and are not identifiable in real time with certainty; many apparent shakeouts turn out to be the start of further declines.
concept.example: Near the end of a four-month base, a stock plunges 12% under the range low in two days on heavy volume, then reclaims the range within a week; a quiet retest on shrinking volume completes the terminal shakeout.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
